summary: No single body tracks AI adoption across America's hundreds of thousands of congregations - coverage comes from research firms, faith-tech platforms, and academic institutes, and this page names them rather than pretending a census exists. Sermon research, translation, accessibility, and administration are the working uses; every tradition is writing its own guidance.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey places churches and faith organisations within the broader "Other services" category under NAICS 81, where 11.3 percent of firms reported using AI in the latest period, down slightly from 11.6 percent in the prior period. This figure covers religious organisations alongside other service businesses in the same code, so it offers a directional signal rather than a precise read on congregations alone. No better official measure currently exists for this sector specifically, and the sourced points here say less rather than speculating beyond what the data support.

On the ground, the closest window into how congregations are actually deploying AI comes from Gloo, a technology platform used by thousands of US churches. Gloo describes its offering as values-aligned AI for missional leaders, providing models, developer tools, and benchmarks built around what it calls seven research-backed dimensions of human flourishing. Its platform supports inference, retrieval-augmented generation, and assistant workflows, and it positions AI as enabling next-generation ministry workflows, knowledge graphs for unifying siloed congregational data, and specialized agents that coordinate tasks across faith-based organisations. The company frames the core problem as one of trust and alignment rather than raw capability, arguing that missional organisations need AI that reflects their values rather than generic commercial models.

The ethical questions surrounding AI in religious life are receiving serious institutional attention. AI and Faith, an interfaith nonprofit, describes its mission as equipping people of faith to bring time-tested religious values to the ethical AI conversation, arguing that issues of control, power, privacy, bias, and economic well-being are at root deeply moral questions. The organisation notes that 85 percent of the world's population claims a religious affiliation, making the stakes of AI development a spiritual matter for the majority of humanity. At the University of Notre Dame, Meghan Sullivan, who leads a research project on AI and religion, has argued that using AI to draft anything spoken in worship reflects a basic misunderstanding of what Christians believe is happening when a preacher delivers a homily, a position that illustrates how theological convictions are shaping the boundaries leaders draw around AI use. Sullivan has also noted that Pope Leo XIV has committed substantial attention to AI challenges, drawing an explicit parallel to Leo XIII's 1891 encyclical on the Industrial Revolution.

The Barna Group, a Christian research organisation, tracks AI adoption, perception, and use quantitatively among US congregations and ministry leaders through its State of the Church work, making it the closest available source to sector-wide survey data on how pastors are navigating these questions. The Hartford Institute for Religion Research, with a 45-year history of surveying congregational trends and digital adoption, and Pew Research Center's Religion and Public Life programme, which periodically measures how clergy and the public view technology in religious spaces, round out the research infrastructure monitoring this sector. None of their specific numerical findings on AI are reproduced in the source excerpts available here, so this analysis does not attribute figures to them beyond their institutional roles.

For an organisation deciding whether to deploy AI, the picture that emerges is one of genuine early adoption, significant theological caution about the boundaries of appropriate use particularly around preaching and pastoral care, and a small but developing ecosystem of faith-specific vendors attempting to address alignment concerns that generic enterprise tools do not. The regulatory posture is currently driven by religious bodies and ethics organisations rather than government, with the Catholic Church's new papal teaching representing the most prominent formal institutional response. Decision-makers in this sector should weigh not only the administrative and operational efficiency cases for AI, which Gloo and similar platforms emphasise, but also the deeply held convictions among clergy and congregants about which human roles should remain beyond automation.
